analysis.summary_en: Background Nipah virus (NiV) is a priority zoonotic pathogen causing high-fatality outbreaks. Methods We conducted a systematic review of NiV outbreak investigations in Bangladesh and India, searching PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and grey literature through 28 February 2026. Case-level offspring counts from 27 eligible sources (323 cases across 67 outbreaks) were used as input to a hierarchical Bayesian negative binomial offspring distribution model. Results Pooling across 67 outbreaks, we estimated a median reproduction number of 0.46 (95% CrI: 0.28–0.73), an offspring dispersion parameter of 0.07 (0.05–0.10), and a serial interval of 13.3 days (95% CI: 12.8–13.8). This epidemiological profile supports targeted containment measures, including contact tracing and quarantine, for effective NiV outbreak control. Conclusion NiV transmission is self-limiting on average and highly overdispersed, suggesting that a disproportionate share of onward transmission arises from a small number of cases. Country-stratified median reproduction numbers were 0.48 (0.23–0.97) for India and 0.35 (0.19–0.59) for Bangladesh, and dispersion parameters were 0.04 (0.02–0.07) and 0.11 (0.06–0.18), respectively, indicating marked overdispersion in both settings.

title: Decoding the diversity: a comprehensive sequence analysis of accessory viral protein W of Newcastle disease virus

analysis.research_question_and_background: Newcastle disease virus (NDV) significantly impacts the global poultry industry, and the function of its accessory W protein remains unclear. This study aimed to analyze the diversity and evolutionary aspects of the W protein in various NDV strains to understand its potential role in virulence and host adaptation.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study conducted an in-silico analysis of W sequences from 1,011 NDV strains obtained from GenBank.
analysis.methods: The analysis involved sequencing data from GenBank, focusing on the W protein variants and their characteristics across different NDV strains.
analysis.main_results: The study identified 24 W-length variants ranging from 135 to 231 amino acids, with the 227 aa variant being the most prevalent. No correlation was found between W lengths and genotype or pathogenicity, but a nuclear localization signal (NLS) in the W was associated with virulence, with 55.9% of virulent strains having an NLS compared to 38.9% of avirulent strains.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight the complex evolutionary history of the W protein and its potential implications for host adaptation and virulence. The study provides a broad view of W diversity in NDV, suggesting region-specific evolutionary factors and host-specific adaptations.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study's findings can inform future research on NDV virulence and host adaptation, potentially aiding in the development of more effective control measures for Newcastle disease.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on in-silico analysis and the lack of experimental validation of the observed associations. The evidence strength is moderate due to the comprehensive sequence analysis but lacks experimental confirmation.

analysis.summary_en: Newcastle disease virus (NDV) is a significant avian paramyxovirus impacting the global poultry industry. The accessory W protein of NDV, generated by RNA editing of the phosphoprotein (P) gene, has an elusive function. This study conducted an in-silico analysis of W sequences from 1,011 NDV strains obtained from GenBank. The analysis identified 24 W-length variants ranging from 135 to 231 amino acids, with the 227 aa variant being the most prevalent. No correlation was found between W lengths and genotype or pathogenicity, but a nuclear localization signal (NLS) in the W was associated with virulence, with 55.9% of virulent strains having an NLS compared to 38.9% of avirulent strains. The study highlights the complex evolutionary history of the W protein and its potential implications for host adaptation and virulence, suggesting region-specific evolutionary factors and host-specific adaptations. The findings can inform future research on NDV virulence and host adaptation, potentially aiding in the development of more effective control measures for Newcastle disease. The study is limited by its reliance on in-silico analysis and the lack of experimental validation of the observed associations, with moderate evidence strength due to the comprehensive sequence analysis but lacking experimental confirmation.
